source.basis: Operator spec page; structured facts only, no operator prose reproduced.

reading.body:
CyrusOne's Houston campus publishes 84 MW of IT capacity, the largest disclosed figure among Texas data centers and 18 percent of the 475 MW the state has published.

That concentration is partly an artifact of disclosure. Only 19 of the 133 mapped Texas data center sites publish a megawatt figure, so the state's 475 MW total is a floor rather than a census. The Houston campus is genuinely large on paper, 84 MW across 347,000 square feet of technical space, which at a nominal 40 kW per rack implies roughly 2,100 racks. But one campus holding the top spot says as much about what other operators decline to publish as about where Texas capacity actually sits.

For AI, published IT capacity is the closest available proxy for how much accelerator hardware a region can host, and it is a coarse one. The accelerator count depends on rack density and on whether the operator sells general compute or AI-specific configurations, neither of which is published. The grid operator, the tenants, the power available beyond IT load, and wholesale pricing are also unpublished. Nothing in the data shows whether this campus has the interconnection or the customers to run AI training at scale.

The data also stops at the present. The campus holds a Green Globes certification, which matters to customers requiring that standard, and no expansion is announced. Houston's rank would move if a major accelerator tenant arrived or if capacity grew past 84 MW. Until then the campus is a reference point for AI demand in Texas, not proof of it.
